Newly emerged Black-tailed leaftosser chicks have an initial wet body mass of 2.45 grams [Ww0 = 2.45 grams], a remarkably low value that reflects the altricial condition of this suboscine passerine. Observations from captive breeding programs indicate that eggs maintained at an incubation temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C] hatch after approximately 16 days [ab = approximately 16 days], a duration that aligns closely with the incubation periods documented in the related Elegant Woodcreeper (Xiphorhynchus elegans). This protracted embryonic development is typical of Furnariidae species that construct enclosed, subterranean nests, where stable thermal regimes are critical for successful embryogenesis. Following hatching, the altricial nestlings exhibit a rapid phase of mass gain, fueled by intensive biparental provisioning of arthropod prey, yet they remain entirely dependent on the adults for brooding and food delivery throughout the early nestling period.

Under the thermal conditions typical of an actively foraging adult, approximately 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], fledging from the subterranean nest cavity occurs at 18 days after hatching [tx = 18 days after hatching], a developmental milestone that signals the attainment of sufficient feather development and neuromuscular coordination for short, clumsy flights. This relatively brief nestling phase is comparable to that of other ground-dwelling furnariids, though it is constrained by the high predation pressure characteristic of Neotropical forest understories. Following nest departure, the fledglings remain in dense cover near the nest site and are still dependent on parental provisioning for several weeks as they refine their foraging skills. The post-fledging period is a critical bottleneck for juvenile survival, as they must quickly learn to locate leaf-litter invertebrates, the primary dietary component, while evading predators such as snakes and raptors.

Sexual maturation, characterized by the development of functional gonads and the onset of territorial singing by males, is achieved at 54 days after hatching [tp = 54 days after hatching] when maintained at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively rapid attainment of puberty, occurring well before the first breeding season for most young, suggests that gonadal development is decoupled from the social and ecological prerequisites for successful reproduction. Field studies indicate that although physiological maturity is reached early, most individuals delay their first reproductive attempt. The first successful breeding event typically occurs at 1.4 years since birth [tR = 1.4 years since birth] under the same thermal regime, a delay that likely reflects the time required to establish a high-quality territory in the crowded forest floor environment and to acquire the foraging expertise necessary to sustain the energetic demands of nesting at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].

Adult females of this species attain a maximum body mass of 36.575 grams [Wwi = 36.575 grams], a figure near the upper end of the typical range for this dimorphic species, where females generally weigh between 34 and 42 grams. This adult mass, significantly greater than the initial hatchling mass of 2.45 grams [Ww0 = 2.45 grams], represents an approximately fifteen-fold increase over the course of development. In terms of reproductive output, females produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], an unusually small clutch size for a tropical passerine, and they typically raise two clutches per year [F_R_i = two clutches per year] during the prolonged breeding season. This low per-event fecundity is offset by extended parental care and high adult survival, allowing for repeated reproductive attempts across several years. The maximum lifespan documented for this species is 7 years [am = 7 years] when individuals are maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a relatively long duration that is consistent with a slow life-history strategy.

Respirometry trials conducted on resting, post-absorptive adults at a thermoneutral body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] measured a basal metabolic rate of 83.64 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 83.64 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value, when scaled against the adult female body mass of 36.575 grams [Wwi = 36.575 grams], yields a mass-specific metabolic rate that is broadly consistent with predictions for a suboscine passerine of this size, though it is at the lower end of the range for Furnariidae. The relatively modest metabolic rate likely reflects the species' sedentary, ground-dwelling foraging strategy, which avoids the high energetic costs of aerial hawking or prolonged hovering. In combination with the extended lifespan of 7 years [am = 7 years], this reduced metabolic expenditure aligns with the pace-of-life syndrome typical of tropical birds, which prioritize survival and iteroparity over high annual reproductive output at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The annual mortality rate, inferred from demographic studies, is correspondingly low, further reinforcing a life-history strategy adapted to the stable, resource-predictable environments of lowland Amazonian forests.
